title: Bloomberg Enables Scalable Crypto Asset Exposure Classification Under Basel Framework
text:
Bloomberg Enables Scalable Crypto Asset Exposure Classification Under Basel Framework
New analytics aligned to the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision's prudential framework help clients consistently identify, classify and report crypto asset exposure at scale
NEW YORK, Oct. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Bloomberg today announced that its Crypto Exposure Analytics now supports customers in assessing their compliance with the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision's (BCBS) prudential standards for banks' exposure to crypto assets and tokenized real-world assets. The solution incorporates enhanced data-driven classifications that enable clients to reliably identify and quantify crypto asset exposure in line with the BCBS framework across risk, compliance, and reporting workflows, without having to stitch together multiple datasets. Originally launched in 2025 to help investors track direct and indirect crypto asset exposures, the solution's expanded analytics help clients bridge the gap between exposure detection and Basel-aligned classification and reporting.
Navigating the BCBS Prudential FrameworkAs regulators begin implementing the BCBS framework for crypto assets, firms are facing growing pressure to consistently identify and classify crypto-related exposure across four categories: Group 1a, Group 1b, Group 2a, and Group 2b. A key challenge is that crypto exposure is often embedded within traditional instruments - including ETFs, mutual funds, equities, derivatives, and corporate bonds - rather than limited only to direct spot crypto holdings.
Bloomberg's Crypto Exposure Analytics has identified approximately 1,700 funds with potential relevance under the framework. Roughly half are funds where crypto exposure is not explicitly part of the stated investment strategy, underscoring the increasing need for scalable, transparent exposure classification and accurate exposure mapping to support capital treatment and regulatory reporting.
Mapping Exposure with Bloomberg's SolutionBloomberg's Crypto Exposure Analytics utilizes Bloomberg's deep underlying datasets across asset classes to surface crypto asset exposure wherever it appears and apply classifications aligned to the BCBS categories. The solution covers 110 spot tickers and currency pairs, 950 listed futures contracts, 320,000 listed options contracts, 670 index tickers, 600 unique company tickers, 280 government and corporate bonds, and 125,000 unique fund tickers.
"For Morgan Stanley, Bloomberg's Crypto Exposure Analytics provides an important differentiator, enabling us to not only identify crypto asset exposure through a robust look-through across funds and ETPs, but also classify our exposures in line with the BCBS prudential framework," said Steven Davis, Global Head of Equity and Listed Derivative Product Reference Data at Morgan Stanley. "The solution provides the exact transparency and classification capabilities needed to support regulatory compliance, risk oversight and disclosure under the framework, while also helping our institutional securities and wealth management divisions more efficiently identify crypto-related products for clients."
"For most firms, identifying their exposure to crypto assets is harder than it sounds," said Zane Van Dusen, Global Head of Risk & Investment Analytics Products at Bloomberg. "Crypto exposure can hide beneath layers of fund holdings, derivatives, and corporate balance sheets, making it difficult to identify and monitor consistently at scale. Many teams initially managed this through manually maintained watchlists and spreadsheets, but that approach is starting to crack as firms work to comply with new regulatory frameworks and prepare for the scrutiny that will follow. Bloomberg's enhanced Crypto Exposure Analytics gives clients a ready-to-deploy foundation for identifying, classifying, and monitoring crypto-related risk across regulatory, risk, and compliance workflows."
Rigorous Data Quality and GovernanceBloomberg applies a multi-layered quality and governance approach to maintain its Crypto Exposure Analytics, including the new BCBS classifications. Classifications are derived through a consistent rules-based process using Bloomberg reference data, securities coverage, fund holdings and company financial disclosures, and are reviewed regularly to account for market and regulatory developments. Each classification includes explainability fields that allow clients to review, validate and challenge results as part of their internal audit and governance processes.
Availability and DeliveryBloomberg's Crypto Exposure Analytics is available via Bloomberg Data License at data.bloomberg.com and can be delivered via SFTP, REST API or into a cloud environment. To learn more, click here.
The same data analytics can also be used within the Security Worksheet {W<GO>} desktop solution on the Bloomberg Terminal via the {WSL CRYPTOEXPO <GO>} and {WSL CRYPTOETFS <GO>} worksheets, ensuring data consistency across both user and enterprise workflows.
Broader Digital Assets RoadmapThis announcement is part of Bloomberg's broader digital assets roadmap to support institutional clients as they navigate both traditional and next-generation financial systems. It follows Bloomberg's joint initiative with Kaiko to develop a pathway for Bloomberg Data License offerings to be accessed on-chain via Kaiko's infrastructure, and launch of a stablecoin dashboard on the Bloomberg Terminal, powered by data from Allium.

Through its Enterprise Data business, Bloomberg provides high-quality, fit-for-purpose datasets that power research, risk management, and execution across the global financial ecosystem.

title: The Next Evolution of ASKB: Your Insights, Bloomberg’s Intelligence, One Conversation
text:
PRESS ANNOUNCEMENT
The Next Evolution of ASKB: Your Insights, Bloomberg’s Intelligence, One Conversation
October 15, 2026
Expanded capabilities enable financial professionals to bring their own IB conversations, Worksheets and files into Bloomberg’s AI, so every answer reflects both the market and an investor’s unique knowledge and context
NEW YORK & LONDON – October 15, 2026 – Bloomberg today announced that ASKB, the Bloomberg Terminal’s conversational AI interface, is now generally available to financial professionals. This is the next step in ASKB’s evolution to provide trustworthy answers based on comprehensive, established financial sources: AI built on decades of Bloomberg’s own trusted data, with newly expanded support for clients to enable content from their Instant Bloomberg (IB) chats, Worksheets and files.
“Every decision made by a financial professional is shaped by more than the market data in front of them. Until now, some of the most valuable information they have, including a trader’s own conversations, a portfolio manager’s watchlist, an analyst’s research, has all lived outside the AI tools they use to make decisions,” said Wayne Barlow, Global Head of Core Terminal Products at Bloomberg. “Bringing an investor’s unique professional context together with Bloomberg’s market intelligence, in one conversation, is what makes ASKB so powerful.”
Easily Find the Signal in the Chat Noise
Bloomberg clients send roughly 40 million IB chats each day. Buried in that volume are some of the freshest, most specific market color and trade ideas a finance professional has access to: their own contacts’ analysis and perspectives on a company, a sector, or a market event. Today, these valuable insights are scattered across a user’s chats and effectively gone by the afternoon.
Now, once enabled, clients can ask ASKB about their own IB chats in plain language and get an answer cited back to the source chat. An analyst or portfolio manager can get a summary of what their contacts said about oil today, catch up on everything that came in overnight, or surface the dissenting view from a bearish contact before making a decision. ASKB can draw on three months of a client’s chat history, tuned for the shorthand and acronyms that make financial services chat hard to search.
Bring Your Security Lists into the Conversation
Worksheets in ASKB let clients ask questions about the securities already in their coverage lists and watchlists. Instead of entering tickers one at a time or rebuilding filters by hand, an analyst can simply ask ASKB for the top performers in a Worksheet, the largest movers, or which firms report earnings this week, and get sourced analysis that draws on ASKB’s existing data, news, and research tools. The lists clients have already built become the starting point for every question, not a separate step before it.
Put Your Own Files to Work
Bloomberg Drive in ASKB gives clients a single place to upload, organize, search, and share their files, from internal research like notes, investment theses, and earnings recaps to the other documents they rely on in their day-to-day workflows. Previously, a file attached in ASKB disappeared once the conversation thread ended. Once enabled, everything in a client’s Bloomberg Drive, including files and folders shared by colleagues, is natively available for questioning in ASKB and remains an available persistent source in future conversations.
Users can ask about a specific file, a whole folder or their entire library and get one answer that draws on their own content alongside Bloomberg’s data, news and research. That opens up a new kind of question: not just what happened in the market, but how it compares with what a firm already believes. Every answer cites the file and passage it came from, and those files are not visible to other users unless the user who uploads them chooses to share with colleagues at their firm.
Why It Matters: Less Gathering, Expanded Context, More Thorough Analysis
Finding the right answer has traditionally meant knowing which sources to check, gathering the data inside them, and piecing it together by hand, often before a professional even knows which sources matter. ASKB does that in a single conversation, grounded in Bloomberg’s own decades of experience in market data, analytics, and industry partnerships, not a general AI model. Client material remains permissioned and distinct from Bloomberg sources. The result: answers professionals can trust, so they can spend more of their time on the analysis itself, not the search for it.
“ASKB is the most advanced functionality we’ve ever built, and it’s also been our most rapidly adopted. Clients tell us it’s transforming how they work, giving them the ability to analyze markets and information they never could before,” said Shawn Edwards, Chief Technology Officer at Bloomberg. “The feedback we hear most consistently is about trust: our users trust ASKB because it’s built on the sources they already know and use, with every answer containing transparent attribution to exactly where it came from. This isn’t Bloomberg building on AI. It’s AI built on Bloomberg.”
About AI at Bloomberg Since 2009, Bloomberg has been building and using artificial intelligence (AI) in the finance domain– including machine learning (ML), natural language processing (NLP), information retrieval (IR), time-series analysis, generative models, and agentic AI architectures – to help process and organize the ever-increasing volume of structured and unstructured financial information. With this technology, Bloomberg is developing new ways for financial professionals and business leaders to derive valuable intelligence and actionable insights from high-quality financial information and make more informed business decisions.
For more than four decades, the Bloomberg Terminal has revolutionized the financial services industry by bringing transparency and innovation to the capital markets. Trusted by the world’s most influential decision-makers, the Terminal provides real-time access to news, data, insights and trading tools that help our customers turn knowledge into action.
Bloomberg is a global leader in business and financial information, delivering trusted data, news, and insights that bring transparency, efficiency, and fairness to markets. The company helps connect influential communities across the global financial ecosystem via reliable technology solutions that enable our customers to make more informed decisions and foster better collaboration. title: Beyond the benchmark: Using advanced analytics to navigate fixed income trading costs
text:
ARTICLE
Beyond the benchmark: Using advanced analytics to navigate fixed income trading costs
Financial Services
Regulation
October 13, 2026
Bloomberg Professional Services
KEY TAKEAWAYS
Liquidity in fixed income is complex. Data can be sparse and stale. Building useful analytics requires a relentless focus on data quality.
There is no one-size-fits-all benchmark because context is everything.
Minimizing trading costs is not about chasing the tightest quote, it is about managing information, market impact and achieving the best outcome.
Advanced predictive tools and modeled liquidity scoring are not here to replace human execution, but to refine trader judgment and provide pre-trade context.
This article was written by Mike Googe and Eman Abd Allah, BTCA product managers at Bloomberg.
Anyone who has spent time on a fixed income desk has probably rolled their eyes at the latest pitch for a “revolutionary”, AI-powered, transaction cost analysis (TCA) model. Most of these models were built for centralized, high-volume equity markets and then retrofitted for fixed income as an afterthought. But bonds aren’t equities. They don’t trade on a single centralized exchange where every bid, offer and print is printed in microseconds. They trade in a highly complex, over-the-counter world where liquidity is dispersed across a maze of venues, protocols and relationship-driven dealer networks.
PRODUCT MENTIONS
Post-trade TCA
However, despite the skepticism, the demand for more sophisticated analytics continues to grow. The continued electronification of fixed income markets, combined with increasing pressure to improve execution quality, is driving investment in advanced trading analytics. The challenge is not whether analytics have a role to play, but how they can be designed to reflect the realities of fixed income markets.
How can you better assess execution quality?
Explore how Bloomberg Transaction Cost Analysis (BTCA) helps identify trends and support best execution.
This article explores the practical challenges of building effective fixed income analytics, selecting appropriate benchmarks across different trading scenarios and understanding how predictive analytics are reshaping transaction cost analysis.
The raw reality of fixed income analytics
Data quality remains one of the fundamental challenges in fixed income analytics. Any model is only as good as the raw material on which it is built. In fixed income, that raw material is often sparse, fragmented, flat-out stale or incomplete.
For firms trading high-yield corporate bonds or emerging market debt, for example, continuous real-time pricing is rarely available. Instead, price discovery is often uncertain and episodic, making it difficult to build models that accurately reflect current market conditions. A model built on historical observations can therefore create a false sense of precision right up until the moment volatility spikes. When the market comes under stress, dealer inventories shrink, risk appetites often dry up and those historical relationships break down in minutes.
Just throwing RFQs out to the entire street in pursuit of incremental price improvement can backfire by causing information leakage and market impact. In credit, the goal is rarely to find the single best “quoted” price. It is to get the trade done in order to achieve the best outcome.
These challenges are driving the development of more sophisticated analytical approaches. Rather than relying solely on historical spreads or transaction data, modern liquidity scoring models increasingly incorporate measures such as dealer responsiveness, quote behavior, hit ratios and prevailing market conditions to provide a more complete picture of execution quality.
The objective is not to eliminate uncertainty, but to provide traders with better context rather than false certainty.
Benchmarking in context: Setting the right measurement
Applying a single, rigid benchmark across the entire order flow will not tell a real trading story. Meaningful performance analysis requires benchmarks that reflect the context of each trade, including the characteristics of the order, the security and prevailing market conditions.
Security characteristics, such as a bond’s maturity profile, are fundamental to benchmark selection. Short-dated issues, where interest-rate sensitivity is minimal, are less likely to exhibit price fluctuations. In these cases, performance analysis can focus on immediate execution slippage. However, as the maturity profile extends to longer terms, duration risk and rate sensitivity introduce increasing uncertainty during the execution window.
Evaluating performance therefore requires duration-weighted analytics and implementation shortfall metrics to account for this and other security-specific characteristics such as coupon structure as well as security types.
Liquidity and the order notional size of the issue further dictate benchmark choice. Highly liquid securities with tight spreads may be well suited to automated, algorithmic execution and therefore measured against arrival prices or model-based references like Bloomberg’s CBBA.
Conversely, when stepping into illiquid corporate or high-yield securities, trading shifts from electronic methods to voice protocols and deep dealer relationships. Performance analysis in these instances will likely require relative valuation techniques, model-derived references, peer-group comparisons and RFQ-specific analytics.
The bond’s specific market structure and the quality of price discovery ultimately determine what constitutes an appropriate benchmark. In a highly transparent market structure, price discovery is continuous and highly visible, enabling traders to automate workflows and benchmark against real-time composite references without tolerating operational drag.
However, as market structure becomes more complex and price discovery degrades, observable market prices become highly limited. In these opaque environments, benchmark selection must shift away from observable transaction data toward relative valuation models, model-derived references and trader expertise to identify the most appropriate source of liquidity.
Ultimately, benchmark selection should be driven by the question being asked. Different benchmarks measure different aspects of execution performance, and no single measure captures every dimension of trading quality.
Effective analysis therefore depends on selecting the appropriate benchmark for the trading scenario while recognizing the limitations imposed by market structure, data quality and price transparency.
Next generation tools
The ongoing electronification of fixed income is fundamentally shifting how trading is done, while also providing the data foundation to build much smarter tools. Multi-dealer platforms, aggregated quote engines and improved post-trade transparency have created richer, more granular datasets.
The industry is moving past static, post-trade reporting toward predictive, pre-trade analytics.
Modern desks are increasingly using modeling and machine-learning-based liquidity scoring to anticipate execution hurdles before an order is even sent to a venue. By combining historical trading patterns, dealer hit ratios, quote behavior and current market conditions, these models can simulate and compare execution paths, allowing firms, for example, to evaluate the trade-offs between a broad electronic RFQ and a bilateral voice trade with a key relationship dealer.
Yet, as these tools become more sophisticated, they bring new risks. Algorithms designed for quiet markets can have unintended consequences or freeze up when volatility surges. The future of fixed income trading is therefore unlikely to be fully automated. Instead, the greatest value is likely to come from combining advanced analytics with human expertise, enabling traders to make better-informed decisions while retaining the judgment needed to navigate changing market conditions.
A data-driven future, grounded in judgement
Advanced analytics are becoming an increasingly important part of fixed income markets. The ability to quantify liquidity conditions, benchmark executions intelligently and anticipate trading challenges provides a meaningful advantage in increasingly complex markets.
At the same time, analytics should complement, not replace, trader expertise. Their greatest value lies in providing context, identifying patterns and supporting decision-making. Even the most sophisticated models remain constrained by the quality of the underlying data and the assumptions on which they are built. Human judgment therefore remains essential, particularly in fragmented and rapidly changing markets.
The firms best positioned to succeed will be those that combine analytical rigor with practical market experience. By recognizing both the strengths and limitations of data-driven models, market participants can better navigate evolving market structures, manage trading costs more effectively and ultimately deliver greater value to their investors.
How can Bloomberg help
Bloomberg’s Post-Trade Analytics and Transaction Cost Analysis tools, powered by BTCA, help firms understand not just what a trade cost, but why it performed the way it did, transforming post-trade insights into better future execution and investment decisions.
Independent execution insights
Gain an objective view of execution quality through Bloomberg’s independent benchmarks, one of the industry’s largest peer networks and purpose-built multi-asset methodologies.
Powered by Bloomberg market data
Bloomberg’s Post-Trade Analytics and TCA solution is powered by the same trusted market data, pricing and liquidity intelligence relied on by financial professionals around the world.
Custom methodologies
Bloomberg applies flexible, purpose-built methodologies tailored to the unique characteristics of each market, enabling firms to evaluate execution using the pricing and liquidity measures most relevant to their trading objectives.
Analyze all of your trading activity
Bloomberg combines execution data from Bloomberg and third-party trading systems, enabling firms to evaluate all trading activity, not just trades executed on Bloomberg.
One connected trading lifecycle
Bloomberg connects analytics across the entire trading lifecycle, from investment decision and order creation through routing, execution and post-trade evaluation. By surfacing insights within the workflows traders already use, firms reduce workflow friction, understand execution in context and make better decisions throughout the trading lifecycle.

title: Australia’s superannuation fund flows in climb
text:
ARTICLE
Australia’s superannuation fund flows in climb
Financial Services
Markets
October 9, 2026
Bloomberg Intelligence
This analysis is by Bloomberg Intelligence Senior Industry Analyst Matt Ingram.
Australian fund managers stand to benefit as the value of the nation’s equity market approaches A$5 trillion by 2035, supported by flows from superannuation assets that our scenario suggests will exceed A$7 trillion over the same period. Australian equities accounted for 23% of superannuation assets as of Dec. 31, within a broader 59% allocation to equities. Industry funds remain dominant.
Superannuation assets set to hit A$7 trillion by 2035
Assets in Australia’s superannuation system are poised to approach A$7 trillion by 2035 vs. A$3.8 trillion in June, our model suggests. Market appreciation, which we assume to be 3%, is a major driver, while flows from the 12% superannuation guarantee can add about A$1 trillion. Immigration could add 1.5 million workers who would receive employer superannuation contributions, further supporting inflows. Our scenario also assumes 3.5% long-term wage inflation. This growth is likely to lift the value of Australia’s equity market to nearly A$5 trillion from A$3.3 trillion as of June 30.
Access superannuation data via the BI AUSTA APRASUPERA<GO> function on the Bloomberg terminal.
Click ‘Excel’ to Flex Growth Assumptions | Source: Apra, Bloomberg Intelligence
Request a Demo
Bloomberg quickly and accurately delivers business and financial information, news and insight around the world. Now, let us do that for you.
Stronger flows by wealth, asset managers Listed wealth and asset-manager revenue is poised for a boost through the end of the decade after retail funds garnered over A$40 billion of superannuation asset flows between September 2024 and June 2026, including A$10 billion in the June quarter. Industry superannuation funds attracted a further A$120 billion of net flows during the period. They also gained A$30 billion of Telstra Super assets through its merger with Aware Super, prompting the regulator to reclassify those assets from the corporate-fund segment. Self-managed super funds added A$17 billion of assets during the quarter.
Click for APRA Flow Data | Source: Bloomberg Intelligence, Apra
Fund allocations underscore bullishness
Australian superannuation fund allocations remained bullish in March, with 59% earmarked to equities, 6.4% to property, and 1.1% to alternative assets. Fixed income apportionment fell to 18.9% from more than 20% two years ago. Industry fund equity holdings fell to an average 57% in March from 59% in December. We think industry flows of more than A$100 billion by 2035 will be a big driver of equity markets locally.
Aussie Superannuation Asset Breakdown | Source: Bloomberg Intelligence
Industry funds extend superannuation dominance
Retail superannuation funds, including those operated by listed wealth and asset managers such as Magellan, AMP and Challenger, gained ground in June, with market share rising to 19.9% from 19.8% a year ago. Industry funds’ share rose yet again and now comprise nearly 40% of total superannuation assets. Public-sector funds’ share stabilized at about 18%, while self-managed funds lost 110 basis points of share vs. March. Corporate funds recorded outflows of more than A$30 billion following Telstra Super’s merger with Aware Super, which likely prompted the regulator to reclassify those assets in the June data.
Australian Superannuation Market Share | Source: Bloomberg Intelligence, Apra
Materials lead 2026 returns on rerating
Australian materials stocks delivered a 25% year-to-date total return through Aug. 31, the strongest in the S&P/ASX 200, while the broader market excluding the sector fell 3%. Rerating and margin expansion drove most of the gain, according to an analysis of the S&P/ASX 200 Index via the Bloomberg terminal’s ASKB<GO> function. Insurers also performed strongly, as robust sales growth was augmented by a market-leading dividend yield. Healthcare’s 5% decline reflects a sharp derating, led by CSL, which more than offset Ramsay’s 52% rally. Real estate also lagged as revenue-estimate downgrades and derating suggest concerns around potential tax changes. Banks delivered lackluster returns as strong sales upgrades were offset by margin compression, contrasting with our view of stronger earnings in 2027.

title: Global insight: Xi-Modi face limits on forging closer ties
text:
ARTICLE
Global insight: Xi-Modi face limits on forging closer ties
Markets
Regional Analysis
Trading
October 8, 2026
Bloomberg Economics
This analysis is by Bloomberg Economics Geoeconomics Analyst Chetna Kumar and Senior Geoeconomics Analyst Adam Farrar. It appeared first on the Bloomberg Terminal.
Pressures from US tariffs and the Iran war have added incentives for Chinese President Xi Jinping and Prime Minister Narendra Modi to expand economic engagement when they meet at the Sept. 12-13 BRICS summit in New Delhi. Tensions along their shared Himalayan border, a root cause of recent bilateral strain, have eased. But deep strategic differences and mutual suspicion make major breakthroughs unlikely.
The pending summit between Xi and US President Donald Trump in Washington also underscores diverging motivations for Beijing and New Delhi: China is eager to demonstrate its global economic reach, while India is concerned about showing too much alignment with Beijing.
Bloomberg webinar: India at an inflection point
Join senior experts from Bloomberg Economics and BloombergNEF to explore India’s growth, geopolitical positioning, technology ambitions and energy transition.
The pending summit between Xi and US President Donald Trump in Washington also underscores diverging motivations for Beijing and New Delhi: China is eager to demonstrate its global economic reach, while India is concerned about showing too much alignment with Beijing.
Xi is reportedly leading a large business delegation to the BRICS summit on Sept. 12-13 on his first visit to India since 2019, sending a message of economic and commercial stabilization as both sides seek to build on the cautious normalization underway since 2024.
India is likely to push for more reliable access to critical Chinese inputs and greater reciprocity for Indian companies operating in China. Beijing wants India to further ease restrictions on Chinese business travelers, imports and investment.
But national security concerns will continue to limit cooperation. New Delhi remains wary of critical dependencies on China and security risks posed by Chinese companies, technology and personnel. It will also be careful not to signal deeper alignment with Beijing, as it seeks to stabilize relations with the US.
Stabilizing the border
India and China have stepped up efforts to stabilize their disputed border and are strengthening mechanisms for senior-level military talks and day-to-day border management.
Senior military talks took place along their shared border as recently as this week, which followed a series of high-level discussions between defense and national security officials. The talks signal a desire to lower tensions, however neither side has claimed any substantive outcomes.
The two sides are exploring an “early harvest” in boundary negotiations. The effort appears serious, but they remain at the beginning of a process to clarify a frontier that has eluded settlement for decades. For New Delhi, sustained border stability remains a prerequisite for broader normalization.
Trade and investment
Economic ties have gradually improved since 2024, but normalization remains selective. India wants more reliable access to Chinese inputs and technology to support its manufacturing ambitions, while Beijing wants fewer restrictions on Chinese companies and investment. China’s tightened controls on rare-earth magnets, battery cells and semiconductor technology pose challenges for Indian industry.
Trade remains heavily imbalanced, with India’s deficit with China exceeding $100 billion in 2025. Indian industry remains highly dependent on Chinese inputs. Electronics, machinery, organic chemicals and plastics account for roughly 80% of imports from China. Indian companies also face significant barriers in the Chinese market.
India is cautiously reopening the door to Chinese investment. In March, New Delhi relaxed restrictions imposed after the 2020 border clashes. That allowed non-controlling Chinese investments of up to 10% without government approval and introduced a 60-day approval timeline in specified sectors including electronics, capital goods and solar cells. It also opened some critical power tenders to Chinese equipment manufacturers with factories in India.
Beijing is likely to press for further easing as Chinese companies seek a larger role in electronics, EVs, batteries, solar and industrial equipment. But China is also cautious about transferring technology and manufacturing capabilities to India without a durable role for Chinese companies. The fear is that over time India will use Chinese technology to improve its domestic manufacturing, reduce dependence on Chinese suppliers, and eventually emerge as a competitor in key industries.
For New Delhi, national security concerns will continue to set the limits. India faces a tension between leveraging Chinese capital, technology and expertise to strengthen its own manufacturing base and limiting strategic dependence on Chinese companies and technology. TikTok remains banned in India, and New Delhi recently stalled a proposed link between UPI — its domestic digital payments system — and Alipay+ over security, privacy and data concerns.
An increasingly unpredictable geopolitical environment and vacillating US pressure has given India and China greater incentive to institutionalize stability on the border and advance cooperation where interests overlap, at least for now. But structural differences and mutual suspicion remain and will continue to pose a downside risk to the relationship.

title: Cash now, repo next: Planning for the U.S. Treasury clearing transition
text:
ARTICLE
Cash now, repo next: Planning for the U.S. Treasury clearing transition
Financial Services
Regulation
October 8, 2026
Bloomberg Professional Services
This article was written by Derek Kleinbauer, Bloomberg’s Global Head of Fixed Income & Equities Electronic Markets Product and Russ Benham, Bloomberg’s Global Head of Public Policy & Corporate Affairs. The U.S. Treasury market is the deepest and most liquid bond market in the world, sitting at the center of global fixed income markets. The SEC’s clearing rule is a significant structural change, and the path to implementation is complex, requiring meaningful industry coordination.
PRODUCT MENTIONS
Fixed Income Trading
Execution Management
The industry is making progress, and momentum is building ahead of the cash clearing deadline at year-end, while much of the done-away infrastructure the repo market will need is still being developed. Bloomberg is working with clients now to navigate the transition and prepare for the broader move to central clearing.
What trading opportunities are you missing across markets?
Unlock the full power of your trading with Bloomberg. Get started today.
An evolving clearing landscape Nearly three years in, the landscape looks very different than it did when the rule was finalized in December 2023. When it was first adopted, the Fixed Income Clearing Corporation (FICC) was the only clearing agency for U.S. Treasuries. Since then, two more have registered, CME Securities Clearing (CMESC) and ICE Clear Credit, giving firms a choice of where to clear. The timeline also shifted in February 2025, when the SEC extended the compliance dates by one year, citing the need for more time to resolve implementation issues and prepare for compliance. Cash Treasury clearing is now required by December 31, 2026, and repo clearing by June 30, 2027.
Which transactions are subject to treasury central clearing?
The Clearing Rule directs a Covered Clearing Agency (CCA) to require its members (direct participants) to centrally clear certain “eligible secondary market transactions.”
Repo: a repurchase or reverse repurchase agreement collateralized by US Treasury securities in which one of the counterparties is a direct participant.
Cash: A purchase or sale, between a direct participant and: (a) any counterparty, if the direct participant brings together multiple buyers and sellers using a trading facility (such as a limit order book) and is a counterparty to both the buyer and the seller in two separate transactions; or (b) a registered broker-dealer, government securities broker, or government securities dealer.
For repo, this captures nearly all trades where a direct participant is a counterparty. The cash mandate is narrower, covering trades where a direct participant acts as an interdealer broker and trades between direct participants and dealers, leaving most dealer-to-client activity out of scope.
The rule also excludes certain transactions entirely, such as those with central banks and sovereign entities, along with qualifying inter-affiliate activity for repo.
Both the industry and regulators are still working through meaningful implementation questions. The SEC, for example, is weighing requests for relief on inter-affiliate (a trade between two legal entities within the same corporate group) and extraterritorial (how far the rule reaches trades between non-U.S. parties outside the U.S.) transactions, which will shape how much activity the mandate ultimately captures.
Building done-away clearing workflows
Beyond scope, the industry is working to address the operational reality of building done-away workflows and what a multi-CCA market means in practice. In a done-away model, a firm trades with one broker but clears through a separate, designated clearing provider, similar to the give-up model in derivatives markets. Making it work may require a pre-trade check, the infrastructure for which has been in place on Bloomberg since the launch of its Swap Execution Facility.
“Having these controls integrated directly into the trading workflow can help firms reduce operational complexity, gain greater certainty around clearing eligibility before a trade is executed and more efficiently manage relationships across multiple clearing providers,” said Derek Kleinbauer, Global Head, Fixed Income and Equity E-Trading Product at Bloomberg.
Done-away differs from the widely used done-with model, where a single broker executes and clears.
Why repo clearing is the next major challenge
At the outset, most firms are expected to build on existing clearing relationships and workflows. For example, on the Treasury cash side, most interdealer trading appears well positioned for the mandate, as many participants have either transitioned to clearing or have plans in place ahead of the year-end deadline. Looking ahead, the repo clearing deadline (June 30, 2027) brings a broader share of the market into scope across a more diverse set of participants. Most firms are initially expected to rely on established sponsored and done-with models while done-away workflows continue to develop. As done-away models mature, the Treasury clearing framework is likely to keep evolving as firms consider a multi-CCA environment, clearing costs, and potential cross-margining benefits. Over time, firms may even choose to clear more than the mandate requires, including cash trades beyond the scope of mandatory clearing.
Bloomberg has continued to build for what comes next. From clearing agency selection at the point of trade to the done-away workflows and credit checks, Bloomberg is well positioned to support clients as they adapt to the implementation of Treasury clearing/the Treasury clearing mandate going into place.

Bloomberg Electronic Markets Brings Automation to its Japanese Government Bond Market-on-Close Functionality
TOKYO, Oct. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Bloomberg announced the first successful fully automated Japanese Government Bond (JGB) Market-on-Close trade, following the introduction of a new workflow. Aligned to BB3P (Hikene Trading), the Market-on-Close reference rate for JGBs, the automated workflow helps minimize tracking error and provides certainty of execution at a specific close time.
Available as part of Bloomberg Electronic Markets, the workflow combines the Bid/Offer List Trading functionality with Rule Builder, Bloomberg's trade automation tool, enabling clients to define execution criteria and automate order routing based on predefined conditions within an integrated order and execution management workflow, through TSOX.
Yudhveer Chaudhry, Head of Emerging Markets, FX, Commodities & Digital Assets at BlackRock observed, "The ability to combine Market-on-Close execution with rule-based automation is a significant step forward for the JGB markets. By accelerating time to market and enabling more systematic execution at the BB3P market reference, this workflow will help minimize transaction costs, reduce manual intervention, and deliver more consistent, optimized outcomes for investors, particularly during high-volume periods. It is an exciting development for one of the highest volume bond markets in Asia, and we were pleased to collaborate with Bloomberg on introducing the protocol."
"We continue to enhance our global Market-on-Close capabilities, bringing greater automation and efficiency to Fixed Income trading for our global clients," said Norman Tweeboom, Japan Enterprise Sales Head at Bloomberg. "The powerful combination of Bloomberg Electronic Markets capabilities enables clients to more efficiently negotiate pricing while reducing operational complexity in a critical market."
The JGB workflow expands Bloomberg's Market-on-Close capabilities across global Fixed Income, which also supports U.S. Treasuries, Canadian government bonds, U.K. Gilts and European government bonds.

Bloomberg Completes Canoe Intelligence Acquisition, Advancing Strategy to Transform Private Markets Investing
October 01, 2026
As public and private markets converge, this acquisition accelerates Bloomberg’s ability to serve investors across both markets, from pre-investment to portfolio oversight, with AI-driven insights
Bloomberg today announced the completion of its acquisition of Canoe Intelligence (“Canoe”), a leading AI-powered data management and intelligence platform for automating private markets data collection and delivery. The successful transaction marks the next step in Bloomberg’s strategy to transform how institutional investors engage with private markets — accelerating Bloomberg’s ability to deliver unified data, analytics, and tools to power end-to-end workflows across public and private markets.
As private markets become a larger part of institutional portfolios, investors increasingly need to evaluate public and private opportunities together and understand how each contributes to portfolio outcomes. Canoe acts as a translation layer for unstructured private markets information, automating the collection and validation of data and delivering it in a structured, portfolio-ready format into downstream systems such as Bloomberg PORT Enterprise. Today, joint clients can immediately benefit from this existing integration, with permissioned and validated private fund data from Canoe flowing directly into PORT Enterprise to support a Total Portfolio View across public and private assets and streamline post-investment workflows.
Bloomberg and Canoe: The Future of Public & Private Investing
With Canoe now part of Bloomberg, clients will continue to receive the dedicated service they experience today, backed by increased investment in Canoe’s technology platform. Combining Canoe’s expertise in sourcing, structuring, and validating permissioned private fund data with Bloomberg’s data management expertise, technology, and scale will expand value across the full investment lifecycle for both private and public markets, including:
Advancing Canoe’s Core Offering: Expanding Canoe’s capabilities and global reach while investing in technology and data management to deliver more timely, accurate, and complete private markets data, giving investors greater clarity and confidence across their portfolios.
Fully Integrated Total Portfolio View: Deeper, automated, and more timely post-investment workflow for exposure & risk analysis, cash management, and underlying holdings look-through, all underpinned by an integrated Investment Book of Record across public and private assets.
Enhanced Pre-Investment Intelligence: Extending fund discovery, screening, benchmarking, and comparative analysis across private markets, helping investors move from identifying opportunities to deeper analysis.
Converged Data Infrastructure: Broader fund coverage and more timely performance data normalized with consistent fund identifiers such as the Financial Instrument Global Identifier (FIGI), creating the foundational data architecture to support more seamless analysis and workflows across public and private markets.
AI-Powered Intelligence: Bringing these capabilities together in a permissioned environment within ASKB, Bloomberg’s agentic AI conversational interface, to help investors accelerate discovery, streamline analysis, and generate insights across public and private markets with greater speed and confidence.
Vlad Kliatchko, CEO of Bloomberg: “We’re excited to welcome the Canoe team to Bloomberg. Our private markets capabilities have grown significantly in recent years, and the addition of Canoe’s data, technology, and expertise meaningfully advances our efforts to become a leader in this space. Together, we can deliver a seamless investment experience across public and private markets, with connected data, end-to-end workflows, and AI tools that will help clients make smarter, faster decisions.”
Jason Eiswerth, CEO of Canoe Intelligence, now part of Bloomberg: “Canoe was built to solve one of private markets’ most persistent challenges: turning fragmented, complex data into information investors can actually use. As private markets have grown, that challenge has only become more important. Joining Bloomberg gives us the scale, technology and market expertise to build on what Canoe has created and deliver even more value to clients. We’re excited to keep investing in our solutions while bringing private markets closer to the real-time, portfolio-level intelligence investors expect across the rest of their portfolios.”

Bloomberg Launches Stablecoin Dashboard on the Terminal Powered by Data from Allium

New dashboard delivers hourly updates on stablecoin supply, mints, burns, transfers and velocity, bringing stablecoin data into existing Bloomberg workflows
Bloomberg today launched a stablecoin dashboard on the Bloomberg Terminal powered by data from Allium, a leading blockchain data platform for enterprises. Available at RWAS <GO>, the dashboard gives market participants onchain stablecoin data alongside the fixed income, FX and money market tools they already use.
Stablecoins now account for more than $300 billion in circulating supply and have become core infrastructure connecting digital asset markets to traditional finance, from settlement and cross-border payments to demand for short-dated U.S. Treasuries. Until now, tracking that activity has meant working with a patchwork of blockchain explorers and analytics sites.
The dashboard covers every stablecoin with more than $100 million in circulating supply — collectively more than 98% of the market — along with select smaller and non-U.S.-dollar-pegged stablecoins.
Inside the Dashboard
The dashboard presents stablecoin data in the same interactive format Terminal users apply to traditional market data. The default view compares covered stablecoins side by side on supply, mints, burns, transfer volume and velocity, with current data updated hourly and historical series updated daily. Users can drill into individual stablecoins to see activity across different blockchain networks, switch the view to analyze activity by network, or filter assets by peg type, including fiat currencies, commodities and other stablecoins.
Expanding Bloomberg’s Onchain Data Offering
Bloomberg has supported institutional participation in digital asset markets for more than a decade. Bitcoin pricing has been available on the Terminal since 2014, and Bloomberg today provides spot pricing, reference data, identifiers and benchmarks for 50 institutionally relevant cryptocurrencies, applying the same rigorous approach used across traditional asset classes. Bloomberg’s Crypto Exposure Analytics also helps compliance teams identify direct and indirect crypto exposure across portfolios.
The collaboration with Allium marks a meaningful expansion of Bloomberg’s onchain data capabilities, bringing blockchain-native data into the Terminal and integrating it within the workflows institutional investors already use. It builds on Bloomberg’s digital asset strategy, including a recent collaboration with Kaiko to make Bloomberg Data License content available on the Canton Network. Together, these initiatives reflect Bloomberg’s approach to digital assets: providing the data, analytics and connectivity institutions need as tokenized markets become integrated with traditional finance.
“Stablecoins are becoming an increasingly important part of institutional digital asset markets, particularly as firms explore how cash and assets can move within tokenized financial infrastructure,” said Matthew Parkinson, Global Head of Digital Assets Product at Bloomberg. “Our focus is on giving clients the same rigor, transparency and integration they expect from Bloomberg across traditional markets. The stablecoin dashboard is available today to all Bloomberg Terminal users via RWAS <GO>.

title: Bloomberg Launches Enterprise MCP to Seamlessly Connect Bloomberg Data with Clients’ Enterprise AI Applications
text:
Announcements
Share
Bloomberg Launches Enterprise MCP to Seamlessly Connect Bloomberg Data with Clients’ Enterprise AI Applications
September 29, 2026
Solution pairs AI-ready metadata and semantic context with workflow-focused Skills, giving clients’ AI agents what they need to interpret Bloomberg data correctly and use it across financial workflows.
Bloomberg today announced the launch of Bloomberg Enterprise Model Context Protocol (MCP), an AI access layer for Data License Plus (DL+), Bloomberg’s next-generation Data License offering. Built for the agentic AI era, the solution enables clients’ AI agents to discover, understand, and retrieve licensed Bloomberg data across more than 100 million securities and over 50,000 fields through a standardized MCP interface, helping firms move quickly and easily from AI experimentation to live production workflows.
Most tools can retrieve data points. Fewer can tell an agent what that data point means, how it was calculated, or whether it’s the right one for the task at hand. Bloomberg Enterprise MCP is built to close that gap, combining semantic context, AI-ready metadata, and workflow-focused Skills that will give agents the information they need to interpret results correctly and act on them with confidence, across research, portfolio, risk, and operations.
In practice, this changes how fast investors in the global capital markets can get from a question to an answer. Instead of first hunting for the right dataset and then reconciling identifiers by hand, or filing a request and waiting, users can simply ask for what they need in plain language and get back data that already carries the context to trust it: what currency it’s in, when it was priced, what it connects to. This shift, from time-consuming manual lookup to an answer you can act on immediately, is what moves generative AI from a pilot into something a firm can run in production every day.
“As generative AI adoption in financial services has grown, the bottleneck facing financial institutions has shifted from model capability to data readiness,” said Tony McManus, Global Head of Enterprise Data and Indices at Bloomberg. “We’ve seen agents that reason well but still can’t answer a basic question about a position, because the data reaching them carries no indication of what it actually represents. On its own, a last price doesn’t say what currency it’s in or what kind of price it is. Connections were never the hard part. Readiness is, and that’s what we built Enterprise MCP to solve.”
Key Features of Bloomberg Enterprise MCP
AI-ready metadata and context: Bloomberg’s metadata describes what each field means, how it was calculated and when it applies, along with the qualifiers needed to make a number interpretable, such as the exchange, currency, price type, period, as-of date. A standalone number is meaningless to an agent; the metadata is what tells it what the value actually is and when it can be relied on.
Semantic interfaces over that metadata: That same metadata is exposed via semantic search tools, so agents find the right field by describing what they need in natural language, instead of guessing mnemonics. Entity resolution does the same on the security side, mapping a name, ticker or description to the right instrument and its relationships to the issuing company — so agents don’t hard-code identifier lists. Metadata makes the data understandable; the semantic interface makes it findable.
Breadth of content. Access Data License content through one interface: pricing and reference data across asset classes, company fundamentals and structure, economics and alternative data spanning across DL+ Live and the Qube Datastore (QDS). New content arrives as new capabilities for already connected agents, not as a new integration.
Task-specific tool design: A single security discovery tool and a single field discovery tool cover the content set, rather than separate tools per asset class.
Workflow Skills: Reusable procedures covering point-in-time universe retrieval, corporate action adjustment and revision history, which clients will be able to adopt and extend. The initial release will include Skills to identify outliers in a set of tickers, review trades that breach accepted price deviation thresholds and assess securities and trades for potential sanctions exposure, with additional workflow-focused Skills to come.
Entitlements and audit: Bloomberg validates a firm’s entitlements before returning data on any agent request, under standard Data License rights. Requests resolve against the Operational Datastore (ODS), and tool-level limits cap the securities and fields returned in a single call.
Client-controlled execution: Bloomberg hosts and manages Enterprise MCP, while clients control the AI agents and applications that connect to it, including the models, prompts, instructions and other steering context used in their workflows.
What’s Next
Looking ahead, Bloomberg plans to further extend Enterprise MCP with real-time data, supporting the agentic workflows that increasingly depend on price freshness, from intraday monitoring and pre-trade checks to risk refreshes and exception handling. Bloomberg is also delivering a forthcoming solution for Terminal subscribers, to provide the same governed and attributable access to Bloomberg data found in ASKB, the Terminal’s conversational AI interface, directly into financial professionals’ daily desktop workflows.
Bloomberg Enterprise MCP is an enterprise offering. Clients can license the specific content domains they need under standard Bloomberg Data License rights. Data License clients can browse and access content at https://data.bloomberg.com.
About MCP at Bloomberg
Bloomberg is both building on and helping shape MCP. Bloomberg engineers are the primary authors of proposals that introduce enterprise governance controls into the protocol and allow servers to present tailored toolsets to different clients. Bloomberg started and leads the MCP Financial Services Interest Group, and holds seats on both the board and Technical Committee of the Agentic AI Foundation, which stewards MCP as an open standard.
About AI at Bloomberg
Since 2009, Bloomberg has been building and using artificial intelligence (AI) in the finance domain – including machine learning (ML), natural language processing (NLP), information retrieval (IR), time-series analysis, generative models, and agentic AI architectures – to help process and organize the ever-increasing volume of structured and unstructured financial information. With this technology, Bloomberg is developing new ways for financial professionals and business leaders to derive valuable intelligence and actionable insights from high-quality financial information and make more informed business decisions.

title: September 2026 Global Regulatory Brief: Private credit, credit risk reform and liquidity reporting
text:
ARTICLE
September 2026 Global Regulatory Brief: Private credit, credit risk reform and liquidity reporting
Markets
Regulation
Risk
September 28, 2026
Bloomberg Professional Services
Recent periods of financial stress and the proliferation of risks across the financial system are fueling the development of regulatory initiatives to strengthen requirements and promote international best practices. The following policy developments represent a sample of the broader regulatory and policy coverage available to Bloomberg Terminal customers. Run REGS <GO> to find out more or contact your Bloomberg representative to learn more:
Canada: Bank of Canada maps Canadian exposure to global private credit markets
Hong Kong: HKMA updates guidance on Basel III credit risk framework
Global: FSB Chair warns of risks arising from frontier AI models
Australia: APRA penalizes ING Australia over liquidity reporting breaches
Explore the latest regulatory insights with our outlooks, webinars, research and analysis.
Sign up
Bank of Canada maps Canadian exposure to global private credit markets Overview: Bank of Canada researchers have published research examining the scale and nature of Canadian institutional participation in private credit.
Key finding: The research finds that while Canadian businesses rely relatively little on private credit as a funding source, domestic asset managers and banks have built a meaningful presence in global private credit markets, creating exposures that could affect Canadian financial stability.
Context: Private credit, defined in the research as business loans made by non-bank lenders, has expanded rapidly worldwide, raising financial stability considerations. The Bank uses a broad definition capturing both direct lending by institutional investors and lending through pooled investment funds.
Key takeaways:
Canadian borrowers: The share of non-bank loans to Canadian businesses has remained broadly stable at around 15% of external funding over the past decade, with banks and public debt markets accounting for approximately three-quarters of business financing. This contrasts with the United States, where private credit has emerged as a primary source of financing in certain segments.
Canadian investors: The Bank estimates combined Canadian exposure to private credit at approximately $500 billion as of early 2026, spanning three groups:
Life insurers held just over $200 billion in private credit in Q1 2026, representing around 22% of invested assets, with a focus on investment-grade credit.
Pension funds held an estimated $215 billion at end-2025, around 9% of invested assets.
Investment funds held $54 billion in 2025, up more than 60% since 2020, representing around 1.5% of total net assets.
Canadian banks lent at least $40 billion to asset managers operating private credit funds, primarily in the US, representing around 1% of overall lending.
Financial stability implications: The Bank notes that while these exposures may support portfolio diversification and returns, they may create channels through which financial stress could be transmitted.
A sharp downturn in private credit performance abroad could affect Canadian investors and domestic business lending.
Assessing risks is a challenge as transparency is limited, leverage is difficult to measure, and links to the broader financial system are still being mapped.
HKMA updates guidance on Basel III credit risk framework
The HKMA has issued revised supplementary guidance on standardized and internal ratings-based approaches for credit risk to align with BCBS standards and clarify operational rules.
Context: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) released updated guidance under the Banking (Capital) Rules (BCR), providing authorized institutions (AIs) with refined clarifications on applying the Standardised (STC) and Internal Ratings-Based (IRB) approaches for credit risk. The revisions follow the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision’s (BCBS) assessment of Hong Kong’s Basel III implementation alongside market feedback.
Key takeaways:
Equity investments in funds (STC): AIs using the look-through approach (LTA) do not need real-time data on a collective investment scheme’s (CIS) underlying portfolio, provided the fund’s financial reporting frequency matches or exceeds the AI’s own reporting schedule.
Credit derivatives & guarantees (STC): Guarantees permitting loss-estimation settlements must meet BCR credit derivative eligibility if their economic substance matches a derivative. Contracts under the ISDA Big Bang Protocol remain recognized.
Due diligence & climate risk (STC): Reaffirms that AIs must perform independent credit assessments rather than relying solely on external ratings, while incorporating climate-related financial risks on a best-effort basis.
Real estate collateral monitoring (IRB): Aligns property collateral rules with Basel standards by requiring more frequent monitoring using statistical tools such as price indices during volatile market cycles. Qualified independent valuations are required following default events or material property price drops.
Next steps: The revised guidance applies to Basel III capital calculations, internal credit assessment processes and collateral valuation requirements for authorized institutions. The HKMA will continue monitoring institutional alignment with the updated BCR guidance.
FSB Chair warns of risks arising from frontier AI models
Overview: FSB Chair Andrew Bailey has warned that frontier AI models are creating new risks for the global financial system, particularly through their potential impact on cybersecurity. FSB Chair Andrew Bailey also highlighted broader concerns around rising leverage in financial markets, elevated asset valuations and concentrated AI-related investments that could increase the severity of a future market correction.
Context: In a letter to G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors ahead of their meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, Andrew Bailey noted that the financial system has remained resilient despite economic disruption linked to the conflict in the Middle East. However, inflationary pressures, sovereign debt vulnerabilities, private credit risks and volatile financial markets continue to pose challenges for global financial stability.
Key takeaways:
Frontier AI models are becoming increasingly sophisticated, demonstrating greater autonomy, problem-solving capabilities and potential threat capabilities.
The most immediate concern for the financial sector is cyber risk. Frontier AI could significantly increase the speed, scale and effectiveness of cyberattacks, creating systemic risks across financial markets.
Because the global financial system depends on common technology providers, shared infrastructure and cross-border activity, a major cyber incident could spread rapidly across jurisdictions.
The letter calls for financial institutions, market infrastructures and technology providers to strengthen vulnerability management, incident response and recovery capabilities.
The FSB emphasizes the importance of resilience among critical third-party technology providers and the ability to restore critical systems and data following significant cyber incidents.
The letter states that many jurisdictions do not yet have sufficient protocols governing the development, release and deployment of advanced frontier AI models.
Bailey calls for authorities globally to support the safe and responsible release and deployment of frontier AI models as a priority.
In addition to AI-related risks, the FSB warns that increased leverage in equity markets, including leveraged ETFs and momentum-based investment strategies, is interacting with high valuations and market concentration in a way that could amplify a future market downturn.
The growing interconnectedness between AI companies and hyperscalers is identified as a particular area of concern because it may increase market concentration and contagion risks.
Next steps:
The FSB is examining measures within its mandate to address the challenges posed by frontier AI, particularly in relation to cyber resilience and operational risk.
The organization is exploring issues surrounding the safe deployment of frontier AI models for cyberdefence in financial services.
APRA penalizes ING Australia over liquidity reporting breaches
The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority has imposed license conditions, higher liquidity floors, and a $50 million capital surcharge on ING Bank Australia after self-reported miscalculations revealed multi-year breaches of statutory liquidity requirements.
Context: The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA) has initiated formal regulatory action against ING Bank Australia Limited following the discovery of historical misstatements in its liquidity ratio calculations. The bank notified the regulator in July that internal errors had resulted in its Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) being reported at approximately 160%, while actual levels were lower and periodically fell below the 100% minimum requirement under Prudential Standard APS 210 Liquidity.
Key takeaways:
Remediation and independent reviews: ING Australia must appoint independent experts to investigate the causes of the reporting deficiencies and evaluate broader risk management and governance practices. The bank must create an action plan for remediation and secure independent validation that the changes have been fully integrated.
Capital and liquidity adjustments: APRA increased the institution’s minimum liquidity operating requirement and imposed a $50 million operational risk capital add-on to address elevated operational risk and prudential reporting weaknesses.
Solvency and group backing: APRA confirmed that ING Australia remains solvent, well-capitalized, and supported by parent company ING Group, noting that the subsidiary has already adjusted its cash reserves back above minimum requirements.
APRA stated that the reporting deficiencies indicated weaknesses in ING Australia’s internal controls and warranted regulatory intervention.
Next steps: The additional license conditions, higher liquidity requirements and $50 million capital add-on will remain in place until ING Australia completes the required remediation and APRA is satisfied, following independent review, that the identified reporting and risk control deficiencies have been addressed.

title: Bloomberg Launches Comprehensive CLO Reference Data Solution, Connecting Insights Across the Investment Lifecycle
text:
Bloomberg Launches Comprehensive CLO Reference Data Solution, Connecting Insights Across the Investment Lifecycle
Integrated enterprise offering brings together normalized CLO and loan-level reference data with regulatory, liquidity and credit risk datasets, aligned with desktop workflows on the Bloomberg Terminal
NEW YORK, Sept. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Bloomberg today announced the launch of its Collateralized Loan Obligations (CLO) Data solution, delivering comprehensive, high-quality and normalized reference datasets for CLO market participants. Available for use across the enterprise through Bloomberg Data License, the solution includes loan-level data that gives clients access to insights on every loan held within a CLO portfolio, and can be seamlessly combined with Bloomberg's regulatory, risk, and sustainability data, and pricing and analytics for deeper analysis.
The new solution aligns with CLO data available on the Bloomberg Terminal via functions such as LLD<GO> and CPR<GO>, supporting consistent workflows across enterprise and desktop environments. It is also accessible via Bloomberg Query Language (BQL), and Bloomberg plans to make this structured reference and loan-level data available in ASKB, the Bloomberg Terminal's new conversational AI interface, enabling customers to screen CLO collateral, compare key collateral characteristics, and conduct cross-deal analysis. Over time, ASKB is also expected to incorporate insights from offering documents, allowing users to evaluate key deal terms alongside the underlying collateral.
Bloomberg's CLO Data solution provides CLO coverage with detailed structure and underlying loan-level collateral data across global markets. Customers can access security master data as well as other key information such as identifiers, payment information and deal structures, and advanced data points including coverage tests and tranche level performance indicators. The data supports workflows including deal and tranche discovery, cross-deal analysis, cash-flow modeling, risk assessment, performance analysis, security master maintenance and lifecycle tracking.
While the CLO market has grown significantly in size, complexity and global reach, the supporting data infrastructure has not consistently kept pace. Information remains fragmented across offering documents, trustee reports, dealer runs and other proprietary systems, making it challenging for market participants to maintain a consistent, timely view of the market.
"As the CLO market has grown, investors have had to piece together information from multiple sources, often with different identifiers and ways of describing the same structural features," said Maureen Gallagher, Head of Enterprise Reference Data at Bloomberg. "Bloomberg is making it easier for clients to understand how the security, its collateral and the corporate borrower fit together in one view. That gives them a clearer picture of their exposures and a stronger foundation for investment and risk decisions."
Bloomberg's CLO Loan Level Data package is interoperable with Bloomberg CLO Reference Data, Syndicated Loan Reference Data and Entity Reference Data. By normalizing reported holdings and mapping Financial Instrument Global Identifiers (FIGIs), Bloomberg enables customers to move efficiently from the CLO tranche and deal level to the underlying loan exposure and associated corporate entity, making the data easier to link, analyze and scale across workflows.
Bloomberg's CLO Data solution integrates with Bloomberg's broader Enterprise Data offerings in a unified data model, allowing clients to combine CLO and loan level information with complementary liquidity, regulatory and credit risk data. The solution is supported by Bloomberg's global team of analysts, who source information directly from involved market participants and company filings such as prospectus and trustee reports. Bloomberg's quality control framework is designed to support the accuracy, integrity and timeliness of these datasets, with key metrics validated for consistency across cash flows and descriptive data and outlier detection algorithms used to help identify potential anomalies.
Bloomberg Data License customers can browse and access this content at data.Bloomberg.com, and Bloomberg Terminal customers can enter DATA <GO> on the Bloomberg Terminal and have it delivered via SFTP, REST API or into a cloud environment of their choice. The same comprehensive CLO reference data is also available via Bloomberg's real-time market data feed, B-PIPE, and Bloomberg Enterprise Products. By bringing together data and workflows across the Terminal and Enterprise, Bloomberg is building a comprehensive front-to-back solution for the CLO market. The result is greater transparency across CLO structures and the underlying loan portfolios that support them.

title: NFU Mutual Selects Bloomberg and Clearwater Analytics for Front-to-Back Investment Management Workflow
text:
NFU Mutual Selects Bloomberg and Clearwater Analytics for Front-to-Back Investment Management Workflow
Leading UK mutual insurer gains a modular front-to-back operating model that combines best-in-class investment management, accounting, reconciliation and regulatory reporting
LONDON and NEW YORK, Sept. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Bloomberg and Clearwater Analytics ('Clearwater') today announced that NFU Mutual ('NFUM'), the UK's leading rural insurer, has selected Bloomberg Buy-side Solutions together with the Clearwater platform to modernize its investment operating model.
Managing approximately $32 billion in assets across a diversified range of funds, NFUM will jointly implement Bloomberg Buy-Side Solutions and Clearwater to streamline its front-to-back multi-asset investment management operating model. Bloomberg will provide portfolio management, trading, pre-trade compliance and trade operations - including workflows to support T+1 settlement readiness - while Clearwater will provide investment operations and investment accounting, with Bloomberg and Clearwater jointly supporting the client's regulatory reporting requirements. Bloomberg's strategic collaboration with Clearwater enables NFUM to establish a seamless, flexible front-to-back composable operating model that improves workflow efficiency, strengthens data consistency, and transaction reporting, and accelerates settlement cycles.
"By adopting Bloomberg and Clearwater's integrated solutions, we are building an automated and highly flexible end-to-end operating model that strengthens our control environment, streamlines processes and builds a solid data foundation for our investment reporting," said Nigel Bryan, Head of Financial Control at NFU Mutual. "The solution automates key workflows across the investment lifecycle, from order generation and execution through matching, settlement and post-trade processing. Bloomberg's post-trade regulatory, risk and compliance solutions further streamline operations while strengthening our transaction reporting capabilities."
"Insurers are modernizing their investment operations by connecting portfolio management, trading, accounting and post-trade reporting around a single, trusted framework," said Jose Ribas, Head of Buy-Side Enterprise Solutions at Bloomberg. "Together with Clearwater Analytics, we're helping NFU Mutual and other insurers simplify complex workflows, strengthen data consistency and utilize a composable operating model that can scale with its business."
"Our integrated offerings give investment teams one end-to-end investment and accounting book of record, so they can make better decisions faster and reliably," said Keith Viverito, Managing Director, EMEA at Clearwater Analytics. "NFU Mutual's selection shows that insurers no longer need to choose between operational depth and technological agility. With integrated front-to-back solutions from Clearwater and Bloomberg, clients can build one accurate, audit-ready operating model across the entire investment lifecycle delivered as a service, and the accuracy and auditability their business demands."
About Bloomberg Buy-Side Solutions Bloomberg Buy-Side Solutions deliver multi-asset capabilities across the full investment lifecycle. With a modular and flexible approach, Bloomberg Buy-Side Solutions offer research management, order and execution management, portfolio and risk analytics, trade compliance and operations capabilities. Integrated with the Bloomberg Terminal service, these solutions provide consistency and quality that enable accurate and transparent decision making, informed investment analysis, and scalable workflows across the enterprise. For more information, visit professional.bloomberg.com/solutions/buy-side/.
About Clearwater Analytics Clearwater Analytics is the natively agentic investment management platform built on a single, continuously reconciled investment record. Portfolio management, trading, accounting, risk, compliance, and private markets workflows run on a single source of truth, creating a connected foundation for automation, AI-driven insights, and agentic workflows across the investment process. Clearwater supports more than $10 trillion in assets globally for insurers, asset managers, hedge funds, banks, corporations, and governments. Learn more at www.cwan.com.
About NFU MutualNFU Mutual is the UK's leading rural insurer and offers a wide range of products, including general insurance, life, pensions, and investments. The firm manages approximately $32 billion in assets across a diverse range of investment strategies, including equities, fixed income, multi-asset portfolios and property.
Its products and services are delivered through a network of NFU Mutual Agent offices, as well as through its direct sales and service centres. With more than 280 agency offices located in rural towns and villages throughout the UK, NFU Mutual has become part of the fabric of rural life and remains committed to serving the needs of its members nationwide. NFU Mutual is proud to deliver more than simply insurance. Making farming safer, supporting rural initiatives across the UK and helping to look after the environment are just some of the ways it does that. To find out more about everything it does to support communities, visit https://www.nfumutual.co.uk/about-us/responsible-business.
